fact_text: Meezan Bank began operations in 2002 as an Islamic bank and has since become one of Pakistan's leading banks for low-cost deposits.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan's low funding cost comes mainly from a large base of current accounts that pay no return, which is the core of its deposit franchise.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan's wide branch and ATM network makes customers walk in to open accounts, so staff need less persuasion to convert them into current account holders.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan staffed full-time Sharia scholars in its early years while some rival Islamic banks used them part-time, and this built the trust that keeps customers in current accounts.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan gives the extra income from customers' late loan payments to charity rather than keeping it, a policy that reinforces its Sharia credentials with depositors.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Some Meezan customers accept a lower savings return than rival banks offer because Sharia compliance gives them comfort, so the bank keeps its deposit base even when rates are competitive.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A bank's cost of deposits falls as its share of current accounts rises, because current accounts pay little or no return while savings and term deposits must be paid.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistani banks can be analysed as a percentage-of-deposits business, where spread, operating costs, provisions and capital needs are all expressed against deposits, giving a quick view of future return on capital.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For two banks holding the same deposits and needing the same capital, the one with more current accounts earns a much higher profit, so return on capital is driven largely by deposit mix.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan's operating expenses are low relative to its deposits, close to the top of the Pakistani bank peer group, while the average bank spends a much larger share of deposits on running costs.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan's loan-loss record is described as better than most private banks, while government-owned banks often post large loan losses because of mismanagement.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Around 6% of a Pakistani bank's deposits must be held as a statutory reserve with the central bank, and this balance earns no return for the bank.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A shortcut for the capital a bank needs is about 10% of deposits, of which roughly 3-4% goes into infrastructure and software that can be checked in the fixed and intangible asset lines of a bank's accounts.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Price-to-book for banks rises with return on equity: a bank earning about 10-12% on equity typically trades near 0.5x book, while one earning 25-30% trades near 1.5x book.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst projected Meezan's 2025 after-tax profit at about PKR 70-72bn, roughly PKR 40 per share, after applying a 52% tax rate.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For 2025 the analyst estimated Meezan's net spread income at about PKR 200bn, based on average deposits of roughly PKR 2.75 trillion and a spread near 7% as interest rates normalise.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For 2025 the analyst expected roughly PKR 35bn of non-spread income from debit card fees, import-export and LC fees, and remittance fees.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst projected Meezan's 2025 operating expenses at about PKR 90bn, a cost line he deducted from spread and fee income when estimating profit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Provisioning for 2025 was expected to fall to about PKR 10bn as interest rates decline, because lower rates reduce the loan-loss charge the bank must take.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On roughly PKR 270bn of capital needed to run the business, the analyst estimated Meezan's 2025 return on capital at about 26%, a level he used to justify a premium valuation multiple.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan follows a regular quarterly dividend policy, and the analyst expected about PKR 30 per share for 2025, with a possible uplift in the last two quarters if deposits keep growing.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On a dividend-yield basis the analyst valued Meezan near PKR 300 per share, applying a 10% yield to about PKR 30 of 2025 dividends, with the dividend itself not included in that figure.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On a P/E basis the analyst expected Meezan to trade near 8x earnings, in line with other top Pakistani banks once the MDR earnings hit is absorbed, giving a fair value near PKR 320 on 2025 earnings, excluding dividends.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Historically Meezan traded at a lower P/E than peers because the market priced in a future MDR hit to its earnings; the analyst argued that this discount is now largely removed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In 2023 Meezan traded near 2x earnings on EPS of roughly PKR 40-45, a discount the analyst explains by the market pricing in a risk of local debt restructuring rather than by weak earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In 2023 Meezan held about PKR 1,500bn of loans to the government, which made the bank's value sensitive to any local debt restructuring; the analyst said a price effect of about PKR 150bn was reflected in its share price.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When a government's debt-to-GDP ratio rises above about 80% and it seeks an IMF programme, the IMF often pushes for debt restructuring, which hits domestic banks holding government paper.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Under the State Bank's minimum deposit return rule for Islamic banks, a bank must share about 75% of its average lending yield with savings account holders, which compresses the spread the bank keeps.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The MDR rule is a headwind to Meezan's earnings, but the analyst believes the earnings decline is largely absorbed in the share price already, so the risk is mostly a question of timing.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Meezan faces a leadership transition after a long-serving chief executive, and the analyst urged monitoring whether policy changes follow, including any shift in its digital investment strategy.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: If Meezan's deposit growth accelerates, the analyst said investors could value the stock on an 8% dividend yield instead of 10%, lifting the share price as future EPS growth becomes visible.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Falling policy rates compress a bank's spread but also push savers toward current accounts, so the net effect on a deposit-rich bank's cost of funds can be positive.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When interest rates fall, bank earnings can dip while the P/E the market applies rises; for a bank with a stable payout the share price can still go up, and the analyst argues this matters more to minority holders than the earnings fall.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Banks are often valued on dividend yield, so when rates fall the yield investors demand falls too, which can lift a bank's share price even when its dividend is slightly lower.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Investors should track each quarter a bank's deposit growth and its current-account share, since both drive future earnings for a deposit-based bank.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst expects digital banking to grow, but physical branches will remain the source of depositor trust for the next 10-15 years, and digital-only banks do not yet offer the same comfort.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cash-deposit machines are automating teller work at bank branches, so branch roles are shifting toward advisory functions such as explaining loan options to customers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Meezan Bank - Pakistan's Premier Islamic Bank - Multi-bagger' (YouTube transcript, undated)
